summary: Specifies a profile of the Megaco/H.248 protocol for controlling Internet telephones and similar devices, called the Megaco IP Phone Media Gateway. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a short instruction sheet for how a controller should use a phone-control language to run Internet phones.

questions: how to control an internet phone
subtitle: How to control an Internet phone using the Megaco protocol

tldr.problem: Internet phones need a way for a central server to control their audio paths, user interface displays, and features, but existing control protocols are too general or not designed for phones.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a specific profile (a simplified version) of the Megaco/H.248 protocol for IP phones, treating the phone itself as a media gateway with separate terminations for audio inputs (handset, headset), user interface elements (display, keypad), and the network audio stream.
tldr.outcome: The profile simplifies the design of both the IP phone and its controlling server by defining a standard organization and a minimal set of required features, enabling manufacturers to build interoperable devices and service providers to manage them consistently.

today: RFC 3054 is Informational, providing guidance for IP phone implementation. The Megaco protocol has since been superseded by other technologies in some deployments, but the architectural principles of the profile remain relevant for understanding protocol design for specialized devices.

sections.title: Internet Phones and Protocol Profiles
sections.content:
An Internet phone is a device that sends and receives voice over the Internet instead of a traditional telephone line. The RFC defines how a central Media Gateway Controller (MGC) (the server) should control a Media Gateway (MG) (the phone itself). Rather than inventing a new protocol, the RFC applies the Megaco/H.248 protocol, which was designed for this kind of control.

However, Megaco/H.248 is very flexible and general. This RFC defines an IPPhone Protocol Profile: a simplified, standardized way to use Megaco/H.248 for the specific task of controlling Internet phones. This makes both phones and controllers simpler and ensures interoperability between phones from different vendors.
sections.eli5: The Megaco language is like a very flexible instruction set that can talk to many kinds of devices. This document says how a server should talk to phones using Megaco, so all phone makers understand the same basic instructions.

sections.title: The Phone as a Media Gateway
sections.content:
The RFC treats an IP phone as a collection of terminations (connection points):

Audio Transducers represent the audio inputs and outputs on the physical phone: the handset, handsfree speaker, headset, microphone, or speaker. Each is a separate termination so the server can control them independently. For example, the server can move a call from the handset to the speakerphone by removing the handset termination from a context and adding the handset-free termination.

The RTP Termination represents the audio stream flowing over the Internet. It connects to the audio transducers via a context (a logical grouping).

The User Interface Termination is special: it represents the display, keypad, function keys, and indicator lights. Unlike audio, the user interface cannot be part of a context. The server sends display commands to it, and it sends button-press events back to the server.
sections.eli5: A phone is like a control panel with several pieces: different speakers/microphones, a screen and buttons, and a connection to the Internet. Each piece is a termination, and the server can plug different pieces together or tell them what to do.

sections.title: Control Operations and Capability Discovery
sections.content:
When an IP phone starts up, it sends a ServiceChange message to the server saying 'I am an IPPhone profile device'. The server responds by accepting or rejecting control. Once accepted, both sides follow the IPPhone Profile rules.

The server queries the phone's capabilities using AuditValue commands. For example, the server can ask 'what audio transducers do you have?' (the phone might reply 'handset and handsfree') or 'what user interface packages do you support?' (the phone lists the display, keypad, and buttons it has). Because the profile defines a standard structure, the server can efficiently discover only the features that vary from one phone to another.

To handle a call, the server sends Add, Move, and Subtract commands to create and change contexts. For a handsfree call, it might Add the handsfree termination and RTP termination to the same context. User actions (button presses, hook on/off) generate Notify messages from the phone to the server.
sections.eli5: At startup the phone says 'Hi, I am an IPPhone'. The server asks 'what buttons do you have?' The phone lists them. Then the server says 'connect the handset to the Internet call' and the phone does it.

sections.title: Packages and Minimum Requirements
sections.content:
Megaco/H.248 uses packages to define groups of related capabilities. For example, the Basic DTMF Generator package lets the server request the phone to send DTMF tones (the beeps you hear when you press phone keypad buttons).

The IPPhone Profile requires that every Audio Transducer support the Basic DTMF Generator and Call Progress Tones packages. This ensures the server can ask the phone to generate dial tones and ringing sounds.

For the User Interface Termination, the profile allows support for packages like Text Display, Keypad, Function Keys, and Indicators, but all are optional. This lets manufacturers create simple phones (just a handset) or feature-rich phones (with display, many buttons, and lights) while staying within the same profile.
sections.eli5: Every phone must be able to make dial tones and ringing sounds. But whether it has a screen or colored buttons is optional. That way, a simple phone and a fancy phone can both follow the same profile.

sections.title: Transport and Encoding
sections.content:
The profile requires support for UDP transport using Application Layer Framing, which allows the phone to send and receive Megaco messages reliably over UDP. TCP is optional.

For message encoding, the profile requires ABNF text encoding (human-readable format). ASN.1 binary encoding is optional, allowing for more compact messages if desired.

The profile is minimal: it defines only what is necessary for interoperability. Vendors can add extra termination types, packages, or encoding methods if they wish, as long as they do not violate the minimum requirements.
sections.eli5: The phone and server talk using standard Internet protocols (UDP or TCP) and speak in a format the other can understand. Vendors can add fancy extra features, but all phones must support the basic ones.
